question: Can a scholar rule on a specific divorce case sent by email or through a third party?
answer:
Actually, I got at least four or five questions. I'm summarizing them, and I won't answer them, and I'll explain to you why I won't. So today's second question is why I won't entertain such questions later on.

A brother sends me a very long email about a specific divorce issue between him and his wife, and it says, "Am I divorced or not? Does this count as divorce or not?" And I got many questions from people here: "My cousin did this, my friend did that," and they send me the scenario and they want the verdict. I will never entertain a specific fatwa of divorce on this table. That's not how divorce is to be decided. You send an email, "My friend said this," and then you send it to me because you happen to be living in EPIC, or whatever. It doesn't work that way. **Never, ever get a specific verdict of divorce from a generic fatwa.** Is that clear? I shall never entertain such questions.

I don't mind talking about abstracts. "Does a triple divorce count as a divorce?" No problem. "Does this phrase count?" No problem. But you come to me and say, "Oh, my cousin Ahmad said this to his wife Fatima," and you write me an email. I don't know, did he really say this or not? I cannot pass a verdict on Ahmad and Fatima until... until what? Until Ahmad and Fatima come in front of me, and I hear directly from them, and I can ask them, "Oh, but did this happen? Did that happen?"

So please, never, ever ask any shaykh about a very sensitive issue of any specific nature unless you are asking one on one and you are the person involved. Is that clear? And this happens to me all the time. People come up to me and say, "Oh, my cousin in Karachi told me to come and ask you." Wallahi, I am not exaggerating: "My cousin in Karachi said this to his wife, and he knows that I am in your masjid, and he told me to come ask you." I said, "Go tell your cousin in Karachi to go to his local masjid in Karachi and ask the shaykh directly, and don't come to somebody 5,000 miles away." I need to quiz. I need to interrogate. If it's you, no problem. Come to me and we will have a conversation. But I cannot pass a verdict on somebody that I don't interact with about their specific marriage and divorce.

And remember, never forget the hadith of that lady who came to the Prophet and said, "Ya Rasul Allah, my husband does not allow me to pray salah. He beats me when I pray. And he never prays Fajr." And she gave a long list of complaints. And the Prophet ﷺ didn't just pronounce the verdict, "What an evil husband you are." He said, "Call the man for me." He called the man. He said, "What is this?" And the man explained: "Ya Rasul Allah, I come home tired from work, and I need to go to sleep, and I want to be with my wife. I only have that much time; I want to be with her. Instead, she's standing praying long sunnahs and nafl. And which one is more obligatory: for me to take care of my needs, or for her to pray her tahajjud at that time?" So the Prophet ﷺ said, "Let no woman pray nafl salah except if her husband agrees." For a wife, the priority after the fard is to listen to the husband. So this was gotten rid of.

Was she incorrect in saying, "He gets angry at me"? No, she was correct. But she's giving her perspective. Then the man gives his perspective. Then the question of Fajr comes: "Ya Rasul Allah, I try, but we have a hereditary issue. My family is known for oversleeping." There were no alarm clocks back then. "Ya Rasul Allah, it runs in our family that we try to wake up; we do not wake up in the morning." So the Prophet said, "Then when you wake up, you have to pray Fajr." Meaning, in this case, okay, you are forgiven if you genuinely try. Basically, the woman was correct. She was not lying. But at the end of the day, when you hear the other side, you hear a totally different perspective, and the man was exonerated.

Bottom line: never, ever ask a sensitive fatwa third party. Never email anyone, even me, if you live in this community. Come to me directly. Don't just email, "I said this to my wife." No. I need to quiz you. I need to ask you, "Well, did this happen? Did that happen?" It's a back and forth.

So, second question: there is no question, because I'm never going to entertain specific questions about, especially, talaq, and it should never be done. Rather, we can speak in generics. Go ahead and ask me, "Does a triple divorce count as one or not?" No problem, we'll talk theoretically. But do not say, "Oh, I said this," and email that to me, and then expect an answer over here, publicly even. No, it doesn't work that way. Come to me one-on-one, no problem.
